text:
The substrate is an aryl-alkyl ether that also contains an isobutenyl (prenyl-type) double bond:

Ph–O–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH=CH₂

1.  Protonation occurs first at the more basic site – the ether oxygen – giving the oxonium ion  
   Ph–O⁺H–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH=CH₂.

2.  Cleavage of the much weaker C–O(alkyl) bond (not the aryl–O bond, which is very strong) then takes place.  
    This produces a phenol (Ph–OH) and a resonance-stabilised/tertiary allylic carbocation:

          ⁺CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH=CH₂   ⇄   C⁺(CH₃)₂–CH₂–CH=CH₂  (after rapid hydride shift)

3.  In the strongly acidic, bromide-rich medium this carbocation can:

   • be trapped by Br⁻ to give an alkyl bromide (not UV-active, so it would be invisible on a normal TLC plate), and/or  
   • act as an electrophile toward the very activated phenol that has just been formed.

4.  Electrophilic aromatic substitution on phenol occurs ortho and para to the hydroxyl group, giving two C-alkylated phenols.  
    Because the carbocation is now fully saturated (after the hydride shift), the side chain that is introduced is the
    2,2-dimethylbutyl group.

Thus the two UV-visible products that appear on the TLC plate are the ortho- and para-alkylated phenols:

   • 2-(2,2-dimethylbutyl)phenol  
   • 4-(2,2-dimethylbutyl)phenol

These correspond to option (D); the other options involve either anti-Markovnikov/Markovnikov mixtures that are not expected under purely ionic conditions, or cyclisations that require the allyl chain to be attached to the ring carbon rather than to oxygen.

Answer: D
